egregious

ih-GREE-jus -- stress on the second syllable, GREE. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Egregious is outstandingly bad -- an error or offense so bad it stands out from every ordinary mistake.

The newspaper printed an egregious misquote that turned the mayor's promise into its exact opposite.

Example

In the final minute of the championship, a defender commits an egregious foul: he catches the ball with both hands inside his own penalty area, two steps from the referee.

This is not a borderline call but a violation so shockingly bad it stands out from every ordinary mistake around it. Egregious attaches to errors, lies, and offenses that leap out for their sheer badness.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

shocking: Shocking measures the jolt an audience feels -- shocking news makes people gasp whether or not anyone did wrong. Egregious is reserved for wrongdoing: an error, lie, or foul so outstandingly bad it stands out from every ordinary mistake. A surprise verdict is shocking; the blunder behind it is egregious.

outrageous: Outrageous points at the anger a thing provokes -- an outrageous price or an outrageous claim makes people protest. Egregious points at the badness itself, measured against every ordinary mistake around it. Something is outrageous because of how people react; it is egregious because of how bad it is.

inexcusable: Inexcusable judges whether a fault can be forgiven: no excuse covers it, however small the slip. Egregious judges size -- a fault so outstandingly bad it leaps out. Forgetting a teammate's name at the awards dinner may be inexcusable; printing the wrong winner on the trophy is egregious.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

minor: small and unimportant

trivial: of little value or consequence

Where it sits · how outrageous the wrongdoing is

glaring → egregious → flagrant

glaring vs. egregious: Glaring is a step gentler than egregious -- a glaring mistake is impossible to miss, while an egregious one is so outrageously bad that missing it would be a scandal in itself.

flagrant vs. egregious: Flagrant outdoes even egregious in defiance: an egregious violation stands out from every ordinary mistake, while a flagrant one is committed openly and brazenly, almost daring anyone watching to object.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — e-: out of, from (a form of Latin ex-)

Root — greg: flock, herd (Latin grex, gregis 'flock')

Suffix — -ious: full of; possessing the qualities of (Latin -osus, via Old French -ous)

Put it together: E- ('out of', a form of ex-) + greg ('flock', Latin grex) + -ious ('full of') spell egregious, using the -ious variant of this unit's suffix family -- literally 'standing out from the flock.' For the Romans egregius was a compliment: outstandingly good. English speakers then used it so sarcastically ('oh, an egregious performance indeed') that the irony stuck, and the word flipped to mean standing out for sheer badness. Today an egregious error is one that leaves the flock of ordinary mistakes far behind.

Use the root in a new word: gregarious: The gregarious puppy greeted every stranger at the dog park like a long-lost friend.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Egregious wants a noun of wrongdoing after it: an egregious error, an egregious lie, an egregious violation, an egregious foul. It judges deeds rather than souls -- for a deliberately evil person or plot, this unit gives you nefarious instead, and for harm that sneaks in slowly, insidious. Egregious badness is loud, obvious, and out in the open.
